In some wrestling practices in high school, we had physical training sessions intended to increase strength and speed and mobility. It would be a Crossfit-style drill where all the wrestlers had to perform exercises for 5 minutes straight with 30 seconds of rest for an hour. Some of these exercises included going on the rowing machines, doing pull-ups, skipping with a 10-lb jumping rope, doing push-ups, climbing up and down 3 flights of stairs, and biking, all at high-intensity for 5 minutes each without stopping until our 30 second break, at which point the drill would continue. When I first did these workouts, it was extremely hard for me because I was not used to these high-intensity workouts. I often failed the expectations of my coach. For example, when my all my energy was spent and I could not continue with the pull-ups, he would come to me and start yelling at me to continue just like everyone else. He would be at my face until I got up on the pull-up bar and creaked one up, at which point he would go away to yell at someone else. He told me that even though I thought I wouldn't be able to complete the exercise, he said he would not let me stop. Even when I didn't stop but slowed my pace a little, he would come back and tell me to give my max effort. Sometimes all I wanted to do was drink water during the 5 minutes and he would stop me from doing and demand that I continue the exercise until the break. Initially I felt miserable and wanted to quit because all I wanted to do was be on the mat and wrestle, not do Crossfit, because wrestling was at least fun whereas depleting myself of energy wasn't.  But in some ways, him always being around and knowing that he was watching me really forced me to work hard and in the end it actually got me to a point where I adapted myself to enjoy his encouragements because it made me stronger and a better wrestler. I guess sometimes the end justifies the means.

I do not particularly enjoy having to evaluate others that I know. I have difficulty being critical of those I know, making my evaluations overly easy of them. I don't critique as thoroughly as I might for some anonymous person.
My mother did not allow me to buy an album from my favourite artist. I felt very sad.
Uncomfortable

I used to  be an administrator of an online BBS group, and I was able to cancel or delete the replies or new posts of those who joined the discussion. Sometimes I was strict with those who did not respect others and might delete their online replies. However, I did feel somewhat uncomfortable about that, since they might not be happy with that and it seemed that I was somehow mean to others. I did make some wrong judgements when evaluating their thoughts or words. When that happened, I felt guilty, and sometimes did not want to be an administrator any more.

My friend wanted me to go with him to buy something, but I didn't care if I went with him or not. I would get him to try to convince me to go with him by paying for my transportation or buying me a drink, or anything that would benefit me. I felt like I had control over my friend at that time because I was able to easily convince him to go out of his way to do something for me because he really wanted something from me.

A situation was when I was taking my driver's test to get my G2. The instructor was very strict, and I felt very anxious doing my test. She tended to criticize my every move and never congratulated me if I was doing something well. Throughout the entire test I felt like I was going to fail, and I had constant negative thoughts. In the end, I ended up passing, and my thoughts quickly changed from being negative to positive.
my lab report mark: my mark was lower than that of my teammates even though we used same results. I was so angry.

When I was in one of my courses' practicals, the TA had power over our class. He specifically exerted his power over my group and I, when one of our group's members pointed out that it was unfair for him to deduct marks on something that he didn't originally ask for us to mention in our practical write-ups. When he stated that "I can choose to mark you on this if I want", I and my group felt rather perplexed, cheated, and mad because he was using his position of authority to selectively deduct marks on something that other classes weren't required to do, and be evaluated on. It was unfair.

When I was in high school, there was one night when i wanted to go to my friend's house but my parents refused to let me leave the house. I felt angry and powerless because there was nothing I could do to change their mind. i was also very frustrated at them for not having a good reason for keeping me at home.

I was the director of the Information Dept. of Student Union in my high school. Apart from the routine jobs, I led my team to hold photography exhibition. Even though I was leader, I tried to listen to their opinions even assigned the work according to their abilities and interest. Actually, I don't like being too dominate especially they were peer.

Going into a job interview with a very authoritative potential boss. I felt intimidated, nervous, and anxious. I did not have any power in the situation, and was essentially following her lead in conversation with no opportunity to express my own opinions.

About a week ago a friend of mine came to me for some advice on how to behave with her parents after having a huge fight with them over something trivial. She was very frustrated about her parents never considering as a priority and always being forgetful when it comes to her. She acknowledged the fact that her parents don't care much about her and more about her brother, however she got so angry this time because her father forgot to do something which lead to problems regarding her university. Given that were very close and I have always been honest with her, I told her that maybe her parents keep postponing deeds regarding her university deliberately. At first she got extremely defensive and starting lying (something she uses as a defense mechanism often) about something unrelated to what we were talking about just to change conversation. Then I told her that she should talk to them in a calm manner about their absent mindedness towards her and gradually tell them what bothers her, unlike her usual aggressive approach. A week later, she tells me that they have been more attentive towards her needs and show little acts of love more often, like bring her food, etc.

It was at the hospital. I was doing a blood test. My mother and I asked the nurse whether my mom can be with when I was taking my blood out. I was really afraid and the nurse was in a bad temper either. She refuses harshly and I was very angry at that moment. I felt like that I wasnt able to protect my mom. I did the blood test. While I was sitting in the waiting room, I promised myself that one day I will take over the hospital and fire that nurse.

Supervising a specific area of the store that I work in.  I was in charge of making decisions regarding discounts on defective items, and delegating tasks to other team members.  Although I really enjoyed having that role given to me, I wanted to ensure that I was assertive but not coming off as being "bossy" towards the other team members.

My home country's government (Venezuela) denied me the possibility to continue my studies (through currency exchange control) in Canada and U of T. I'm going to be forced to return to Venezuela after this semester. It felt very frustrating, since I dreamed of coming to this place. It's very unfair, but oppressive governments tend to be that way.

We thought about buying something expensive for our house with my roomates. One didn't want to buy it at all the other was neutral, but I really wanted to buy it. As it was expensive I couldn't buy it myself so I needed their support. We discussed it a few times but since the others didn't share my enthusiasm about this they didn't seem too interested in the subject. I felt powerless about this, I even thought of buying it myself but I didn't because it was too expensive to buy individually. I know they would have used it after we bought it and I feel angry because I couldn't defend my point fairly.

I wanted to get a certain item at the grocery store but it was my Mom doing the purchasing so I didn't really have a say in it and since she wasn't going to buy it for me I had to put it back and I didn't end up getting it. I felt very poorly because I really wanted the item and it was something I enjoyed but I didn't get it because I don't have the power to tell my mom what to spend money on and what not to spend money on. It made me feel sad, powerless and made me feel like my opinion didn't matter.

In high school, I took an orchestra course, and I highly extremely really disliked the instructor. She would penalize us if any of us were late by a few minutes while sometimes she would be half an hour late to class. She would make us take stressful playing tests by memory, which I though was extremely unnecessary as we would obviously be performing with the music in front of us. She was incredibly rude and disrespectful to her students. I hope that I never have to encounter an instructor like her again.
Somewhat nervous and uneasy about not knowing what would happen. Overall demoralized and upset.

In grade 12, I had an interview for a co-op position at the Toronto Police Headquarters. The woman who was interviewing me had power over me, since she was in an evaluation position. Since I really wanted to be accepted into the co-op program, I felt nervous and anxious during the interview (although I like to think that I didn't show it). In the end, the interview went well and I got accepted into the program.

I have organized a presentation about explaining one kind of dances to people. My group have five people and I feel it is very hard to make everything go through when I do this. For example, someone will complains his task is the most difficult and does not want to do it. Eventually, we gave a good presentation, I feel really relax when we done.

When I was trying to do well in school, despite my father wanting the same thing, he made it much harder for me by getting mad with me and telling me I had to do other things as well, such as helping him with hard work in the garden for almost six hours, even though I told him I have a test the next day that I need to study for. So he used his power as my father to yell at me, make me work hard at school, and complete his personal tasks as well. I felt like this is not something a human would do to another human, knowing how hard life can be for a student. I also felt like he betrayed me since he told me he would do everything to make my life easy and make school a good experience, but really said these things for his own benefit.

my friend is not very good at writing. when it was time for writing university applications and essays, she was extremely confused. she was afraid that she wouldn't get accepted to any universities if she couldn't write a well-written essay for university. I suggested that I could perhaps write the essay for her. She was so impressed with the results that she came back with four of her friends. they all wanted me to write some sort of essay for them. I felt in power because I've only learned to write in English for the past 5 years, but those who asked me to write for them were mostly native English speakers. I felt superior to them because I knew I had probably acquired more writing skills in the past 5 years than they had in their entire lives. or maybe they were just lazy. either way, they offered me money. and a lot of money too, for a high school student.
i will control the a fatty person to lose their fit. To do exercise every day,and let her think it is very easy without any effort. It will make me fell happy .
As an only child, I have power over my parents. Whatever I want or need, I will get if I ask my mom for it.
One of my friends was struggling with her homework and needed my notes. So I gave them to her considering they will help her.

when i ask someone a question and waiting for the response, i always feel the person i ask is not willing to share the study method with me. and sometimes when i have to do the things that my mom ask me to do.

I have organized an activity for helping the students who cannot continue their study just because of money. I asked my friends collected the used toy and pack it up to sell at my community. Before I did it, I feel very excited. However, I feel it is difficult to control people's behaviours when I really tried to start do it. For example, my friend's parents felt this activity influences her study and asked her do not continue do it. In the end, we still sell out those toys and make profits. I did not feel very happy as I imaged before.
I was the head of my high school orchestra and was responsible for arranging practices and encouraging those who are lack of skills to enhance their performances.

Running laps at football practice as a punishment. Felt very annoyed and felt even more hatred towards the activity because it was not my choice as opposed to doing it for personal fitness or as a challenge.

An example of this is when I was in high school and apart of my student leadership committee. I was able to help pick and chose who would be apart of our group. I had to sit in on interviews, and ask questions which would determine if the person would be grantee membership to our club. I felt bad most of the time because I knew majority of the people applying and they was about a 100 people and we could only chose 30 so that was a hard job in choosing who would get chosen and who would not be. My thoughts on it is that we should be able to expand the program because even though we are the voice of the student body, a group of 30 people are not necessarily going to be able to get everyone's opinions across accurately. At the same time i understand because too many minds can lead to chaos.

When my ex-boyfriend broke up with me. I didn't see it coming, and in the moment I really couldn't believe that was real and our relationship was ending. We hadn't seen each other very much and so he thought that it'd be hard to maintain our relationship during the school year, since he had different goals he wanted to accomplish (which even now he hasn't even done). I offered suggestions to solve our problems but he dismissed every one with a reason why it wouldn't work out, then after a while he said the ultimate "I just don't feel the same way I used to". It hurt quite a bit. I was trying really hard not to cry in front of him, because I already felt like the weaker person, being broken up with. I was very shocked and upset, but also angry. Angry that he was so cold towards me when things were fine the last time we saw each other. I felt disrespected and ashamed that I was being broken up with (like my pride was hurt). It definitely felt like he had power over me at that moment and even still I feel like he looks down on me just because he was the one to initiate the break up.

When I was stuck in an exam where I had no clue what I was doing, so in this case the "someone" who had control over my ability was my professor who wrote the test. Knowing that the next hour will be extremely unpleasant, I experienced a sort of learned helplessness as I have stumbled through the course prior to this test. I ended up attempting to use logic to power through. However, as soon as the test was over, I felt a great sense of relief and joy that was somewhat odd because I knew that I didn't do very well in the test.

In my high school in Nigeria, I was made the dining hall prefect. This meant that I was in charge of making sure that people had enough to eat and that the food was made in a conducive and hygienic place. During my one year holding this position, I understood what it meant to be in charge and in control. Sometimes, I had to do things I didn't want to but I had to. In the end, it was a good experience.

One example is club tennis tryouts. People on the team are in a position to evaluate your performance. I felt kind of vulnerable and embarrassed if I made a bad shot. However, making a good shot or winning a match/point made me feel even better than winning a normal point (not being evaluated).

I was a tennis coach over the summer for little kids where I had power over them, so I was able to order them to do certain drills, pick up the balls, and pay attention to the other coaches. A lot of times the other coaches and I would bribe the kids with candy, or threaten them with having to sit on the bench for a certain amount of times. It was nice being in power, but at times I felt as if we were ordering the kids around too much. It was also upsetting when the kids showed little or no respect towards me and the other coaches.

In high school, I helped start a dance team. During practices, my friend and I both watched other members perform the choreography to make sure that they were doing everything correctly. If they were doing something wrong, we critiqued their dancing in order to help them improve. The purpose of giving critique was to help the members improve their dancing.
I felt scared and small, like I was working twice as hard to get where I knew I belonged.

When I played soccer for my travel team, I was almost always in a position in which my coach had power over me (and my teammates). He constantly evaluated the way I played and coached me on how to improve. Sometimes when our team was playing poorly or if I personally did something wrong, he would yell and that was never fun. When someone else is in control, I usually am good at following directions and am a "good learner", but when I am yelled at or told in a condescending way to do something I shut down. I especially do not like to be told what to do by people around the same age as me, such as if a teammate told me what to do.

When going through the process of who I was going to live with my second year, I was put in the position of providing my opinion of some of the people with whom I had gone to high school so that we could reduce the number of people in our group. It was a difficult thing for me to do, because even though I like them a lot as people and I would have been happy to live with all of them, I knew that we had to bring our numbers down and I also had to take into account whether or not they would get along with the group. I experienced a lot of conflict in my mind while doing so.

During high school I was captain of the fencing team. Every day during practice I, along with the other captains, ran drills and organized. There was one day in particular in which we had trouble managing a younger fencer. She was talking back and giving attitude, which caused me to be frustrated and angry. She was completely disrespecting the authority we were given and had no regard for her own position. It worried me because we did not want to let the other younger kids think they could get away with doing the same thing. Eventually another captain and I had to go speak with our coach to resolve the situation.

I am one of two captains of the women's club lacrosse team here at UVa and I am in charge of planning practices and determining line-ups for out games.  I have to think about what drills will benefit everyone the most as well as who will be the best players on the field together to bring about win in games.  I like having the influence on the team, but it stressful knowing that it is my responsibility and I have to deal with the opinions and feelings of 30 other girls.

I was president of my school's chapter of the National Honor Society, and one time we had an opportunity to visit an opening of a museum. I was asked to choose 5 people to join me, and I knew that many other people really wanted to go since it was going to be a very fancy and upscale event. When I first heard about the news I was excited but then I started to feel conflicted about how to choose who would come with me. So I decided that I would choose those who had put in the most effort into the work they were doing within the National Honor Society, and asked other members to rate them on a scale of 1-5. That made it easier to choose, it satisfied most people and I felt like I was being fair.

For my senior prom in high school, I was in charge of planning locations, dinner, transportation, and the after party. To ensure that we would have a great night, I assign jobs to other members in the group, such as contacting the limousine service and finding a good restaurant. On the one hand, I felt very stressed because we were running out of time and I did not have much experience at planning, but I also felt comfortable in assigning tasks as a leader. For this reason, I decided to pursue a leadership role by joining the First Year Council.

at club tennis tryout the players who had already made the team had the power to decide whether i would make the team as well. When i didn't make the team i was hurt and angry because i thought they had made a mistake.

As the field hockey captain, I had the authority to run drills and time the girls' mile intervals. Through encouraging the girls and disciplining them at the same time, I gained lots of leadership skills as well as realizations that being too harsh or pushing the team to their challenge point was not the most beneficial approach. Balance and rest are vital for succeeding in a majority of high-intensity sports.

The last situation where someone had power over me was actually an unintentional situation.  Everything I did was judged.  I had to act a certain way, think a certain way, and feel bad about myself.  I entered a state of depression because I was being so evaluated.  But the interesting part was that I wasn't really being evaluated by anyone.  When i came to college, I left someone at home that I cared about.  Now, she has a power over me thanks to me missing her.  I have no power and feel little of myself now that I can't know what she is thinking.

I was once the head coach of a youth basketball team. I did not feel like I was ever on a "power trip," though the autonomy to run my own practices and command the players was satisfying. I felt pressure and responsibility however, as I wanted to be liked by my players and their parents. Therefore, I would listen to the opinions of the players and parents and consider their ideas seriously before acting. In this regard I feel as though I was a democratic leader, but firm when I needed to be.

This past summer I helped lead a mission trip to West Virginia. We had 10 kids sign up for the trip, all between 10-13 years old. We were assigned to construct a roof for a porch attached to a trailer in the Appalachia area. Building a roof with a younger group was very challenging. My patience was definitely put to the test because the kids really couldn't participate much (they couldn't reach!) and got super rambunctious. It was my job to keep them safe in a dangerous place and I struggled to keep their attention and enforce the rules. It was frustrating.

I was working in the nursery at church on Sunday. Obviously, I had responsibility of the kids and therefore had to control the group in order to promote safety of all of the kids as well as maintain order.

Looking for housing for the next academic school year, my roommates and I were looking at our options. There are some criteria that I want the new place to meet, if they're not all met, I would strongly veto the place. Since my roommates want to live with me, they allow me to be choosy and even veto the places they they liked. I feel strongly about how I want the place for next year to be like. So I may come off very headstrong and irrational, but during the time I feel that what I want is as important as what my roommates want. So there are things I'm not willing to compromise.
I have younger brothers. Whenever I am responsible for them I am in a position of power. I have no distinct feelings or thoughts about these situations.
Never really been in a position of power.
There was pressure to choose the best situation. I had to weigh what I would lose or gain from each situation. I was nervous as I tried to minimize negative outcomes and decrease anger towards me.
I was at a flea market and I was able to bargain for a product by lowering by 50% off.

I have a lot of power when I enter the dining hall. I can eat anything I want due to my high metabolism. I can choose between a plethora of options. The hard part is determining what I want to eat the most. I am in complete control of this situation.

I was on the judicial council at my high school. I often had to determine classmates' punishments with my peers on the council. I had a great feeling of responsibility, and I often felt uncomfortable when a friend had to go to council. On one occasion, a guy in my grade had to be evaluated for beating up a student much younger than himself. His actions clearly reflected his immaturity, and I feared that he would dislike me after I had to confront him.

The one time I remember I was in a position of power is when I tutored an underclassman in high school on SAT. By being in the higher position of the tutor rather than the tutored, I controlled whatever my student's next plans and goals were in the future. By being in this position, I felt constant burden and pressure for him to do well in his exams, and if he did not get the problem correct, I would think about what I am doing wrong. Being in this position did not give me any feelings related to superiority or power, but rather I felt vulnerable and prone to mistakes.

I spent this past summer living and working in Ohio to be near my boyfriend who I have been in a long distance relationship with for a year and a half. The only job I could get was one where I was working very few hours and not making as much money as I wanted. When my parents found out how little money I was making they told me that I wouldn't be allowed to return to Ohio next summer. I told them that as a college student who is no longer even living in their house it was not up to them to decide where I spend my summers. They laughed and told me that if that was how it was, it was also no longer up to them to pay for my education either. I felt really angry about it; it seemed like they were flaunting their power over me and trying to control all of my actions. I still don't feel great about it, but after thinking about it more I realized I was being really immature to take their money and generosity and then tell them that I was going to continue doing what I wanted regardless of their opinions.

Recently, my roommates signed onto a rental agreement for next year. At the time I was in a certain class and unable to voice my opinion about the property. Even though I had previously told them that I was unable to pay very high prices for an apartment they went ahead and signed without my consent anyway. This made me feel totally powerless because I was not able to voice an opinion and get them to compromise because they had already done the task. I was forced into signing the agreement because I need a place to live next year but it caused a lot of tension between my roommates and I. They cared little about how their actions impacted me and I still feel as though they care little about my opinion and now I hold a lesser opinion of them because they did not care about the impacts that their decision would have upon me.

I was in a position where someone else had power over me when I was an employee working under my boss at a Chiropractic clinic.  I always strived to do my best work to keep my employer happy so that he was not concerned with finding a new person to take my position.

I volunteer at a day care in Charlottesville and am often able to tell the children what to do and what not to do. Last week when they were fighting over the swings I was able to tell them to stop and that someone needs to get off of the swing and let another kid on. I enjoy knowing that they will listen to me however I wish I didn't have to tell them what to do very often. It's nice to be in a place of power in an atmosphere of such chaos.

When working at my summer job I felt as if my boss was able to control what I did or else I could get fired. She had authoritative power over me, which made me comply to the orders she gave. This made me do things in the way that she instructed. It made me feel inferior to her.

My senior year in high school, my volleyball coach had a lot of power over me. She is really controlling and is very strict about enforcing her rules. One day before an important game, I forgot my elastic band to practice. We used to put the elastic band around our arms to help out passing techniques. I didn't have mine for the drill she wanted to do. So, she made me go practice with the JV team for the rest of practice on the other court. All I wanted to do was play with my team because of the big game that was the next day, but instead I had to be with the younger girls for the rest of the night, even when that drill was over. I felt very embarrassed and frustrated because I didn't feel like I deserved that punishment. Lots of girls on varsity borrowed an elastic band from the JV girls without my coach knowing, so I was the only one who got punished because I didn't do that. It was a miserable day at practice.

We held auditions for the improv troupe I'm a member of this year and we were able to evaluate and judge the auditionees on their performances to decide whether or not to extend an invitation to join our group. This was my first time being on the evaluating side of improv auditions so I felt pretty powerful, thankful, and energized. During the second round of auditions the members of the troupe perform with the auditionees and felt so much more relaxed and confident doing it than I had when I auditioned because I knew my spot was secure. I also knew that no matter what I did in auditions, to a certain extent, there would be very few consequences. This put me at ease and made me much better at improv to be honest.

I had to present my final research project to my Biotechnology teacher. I was nervous to present it because she had a lot of experience in the field and the project that I worked on was very technical. I was worried that she might pick apart my project.

Auditions for college gave complete power to my auditor as to whether I would be accepted into the acting program at certain colleges. It made me anxious to know that my fate for the next four years was dependent on what one person thought of my acting skills. It also made me feel determined to perfect my audition in order to impress them. I was looking for acceptance and gratification but could only be given that by the auditor.

I was captain of the soccer team and I had to evaluate the performance of my teammates. During training I would give them feedback and try to encourage them to do better every time they came in touch with the ball. My main goal was to motivate them to be better, rather than pressuring them. I enjoy encouraging people to do their best work.

The last person to have significant power over me was my father.  I do not practice his religion, however, he still believes that I should attend church regularly.  I feel that I should still attend so as not to disappoint him and make him feel like a failure since it is very important to him that I practice his religion.  Because of this I still attend church with the family.

In my high school finance club I was made in charge of overseeing and evaluating the portfolios of some of the newer members to then give them feedback on how they performed. I felt powerful and in my mind I knew that what I would say would hold weight on how the new members would go on to think of me and the club. With this came a sort of pressure to be fair and not too harsh, but at the same time judgmental.

I was a tennis instructor over the summer. So, I was in charge of children. I helped them develop their skills and taught them new ones. This gave me power because if I taught them poorly they may not turn out to be that good of a tennis player. Yet, if I taught them well, they had the ability to succeed. I really enjoyed this job, and it was quite satisfying.

Last week I had an interview at Urban Outfitters for a job. Obviously I had no control over how the managers viewed me, so I tried my best to look as nice and "trendy" as possible and appear pleasant and likeable. They asked me tons of questions and kept writing notes down on their clipboards and I wanted so badly to know what was going on but obviously they couldn't tell me. I was extremely nervous and unsure about how to feel about the situation overall.

In tenth grade, I was playing the violin in a regional music competition. There were 3 judges who all offered different perspectives on how I played. The fact that there were three judges made me feel more pressured than usual (I have participated in these competitions in ninth, eighth, and seventh grade as well). I felt like there were just two more strangers that I had to impress with my playing. This was kind of intimidating, but I managed to get through my program without making any mistakes. I came in 4th, which made me feel quite proud of myself, because there were several other players from several different states of the Northeastern US there.
When I cold not get into a class I wanted and the teacher would not let me in. I felt like I had no power in the situation.

A position of power I was once in would be during high school when I was one of the coaches of the World Scholar's Cup club. The World Scholar's Cup is an academic competition, much like the international version of the American Decathlon in structure and content. I and my teammates have been participating for several years and as seniors we were called as veterans to coach the teams. It felt very good to be able to have been there and done that and to share my experiences. I liked the idea that I was able to use my abilities to influence others. Overall it was a good experience.
The few times I have felt that someone had power over me, I felt very frustrated.  By very definition, there was nothing I could do and that feeling of helplessness really ate at me from the inside.
I was a captain of my high school soccer team, therefore I had limited power, but it wasn't anything serious in particular.

This particular time was when I was being evaluated for work performance at my job senior year; I was a little nervous, but also excited to see what my managers had perceived me to be.  All that happened was I was called into the manager's office after my shift, and they had an evaluation list for me, and they read off what they had put down for me.

When I was applying to the University of Virginia, I was under the control of the office of admissions and during that period of time I felt very anxious. I had a lot of support behind me, but once I hit the send button I was helpless to improve or change my status in the eyes of the admissions officers. Because there was such a long delay between my application deadline and when I found out if I was accepted or not, eventually my feelings of anxiety subsided. However, they came back again when my friends began to find out if they had gotten into their colleges as well. It was quite nerve-wracking at times.

I had an interview last week by APALTI. It's a group interview of five interviewees surrounded by six other interviewers. I was quite nervous when they threw a question because i knew half of the people in the group and I was afraid that I might not have the chance to get into the program. I was just trying to stay calm and take turns for answering the questions. When the thing was over, I felt relieved somehow. At least I tried.

During one winter vacation, I had planned to spend some days traveling around and visit some friends. But high school teachers decided that an evaluation test would be held at the beginning of spring term. So I had to stay in and do review work for a month. I felt disappointed and probably a little bit annoying because I thought the test restricted my freedom during vacation.

In the application process for college. I applied to a school that I knew was hard to get into and the decision was in the hands of total strangers who would be reading my application. I did not get into the school. I felt like I had no control over the situation and could not get answers or clarifications about the decision or the process. I just had to accept the outcome.

I was the Senior level Copy Editor of my school's yearbook and I was responsible for managing all the staff writers and ensuring that the content going into the book was correct, appropriate and exciting. Many times I would have to delegate different tasks or give constructive feedback, and even sometimes reprimand staffers who were not handing in work on time. When I had this position I felt good about myself and confident in my own abilities. I have never felt smarter. I think it was a very good activity for me to be involved in because it strengthened my interpersonal skills and self-confidence.

I was an instructor assistant at a wilderness school this summer. Together, the instructors and I planned activities for, guided, and generally looked out for our groups of kids (ages 7-8 and 11-14). Being kids, they did things that they were not allowed to do, so our response was taking time out of fun activities to address the issues. We laid out our logic and the consequences of bad behavior clearly, and most kids got it down pretty fast. Of course, there were always the troublemakers, which led to us developing some inventive tactics since the school operated on the principle of guidance rather than blunt forcing. It was a subtle kind of power, but ultimately, the adults called the shots.

I was teaching a karate class and one kid wanted to be first in line. I said he couldn't be because that spot was reserved for kids who were a higher belt than he was. I recall being annoyed with his persistence.

A professor my freshman year of college failed me on an assignment that was worth 15% of my grade. She said I must redo the assignment (only being able to achieve a C at best) or the grade would remain an F. I had worked very hard on this assignment--it is not as if I had slacked off or just rushed to pull it together at the last minute. I was extremely upset, and additionally, it was almost time for finals. I had to do the assignment again in addition to studying for all the finals in my other classes. I felt belittled, unintelligent, and powerless. There was nothing I could do except try again and turn it in for the C. I had no choice.

In high school when I applied for some scholarships there was a selection committee that ultimately decided who received each scholarship. In this situation where I had no power or control as to what would happen, I felt relatively calm. Knowing there is nothing more you can do in a situation is somewhat calming. I was still a little nervous of course but knowing I had done all that I could at that point was calming enough to make me content with the situation.

I tutored a primary school student when i was in high school. Once i could decide when to finish the tutoring based on how the pupil performed. I felt relax with the power because i had to care about nothing stressful, and thought he might be a little bit stressed.

When I was interviewed by college admission officer, I felt that he has power over you. He got to decide whether I could get into my dream school or not. He could decide what my four-year college life is like. I was always thinking how I should behave to please him, to persuade him that I am a good fit for the university. I felt that although I have done all I could to(taking the tests, get good grades in school, taking part in extracurricular activities), I still cannot decide my future path. I felt frustrated and lost.

It was the end of the semester and my grade was on the border and would be the higher grade if the teacher decided to round. I sent a polite email to the teacher asking whether he would consider rounding. I had to wait for his reply and felt relieved and happy when he sent a message back saying he would, in fact, round up the grades.

There was a time when my karate instructor made me do 100 push ups because I was late to class. There was traffic on the way there but that wasn't any excuse for my instructor. No amount of convincing would change his mind. I had to do the push ups or I could no longer attend class. I had no control over the situation and I felt helpless because it wasn't my fault. I could not convince him so I felt that he thought I was lying.

In my last meeting with the exec board of my fraternity. I was planning a social event but it got vetoed by our president and there was really nothing I could do about it. I was angry and thought that the system under which the fraternity operates needs to change.

During student council in high school, I was the senior class president and above me was the student body president. Often times there were things that I wanted done for the school and the student body president disagreed with me and he had the ultimate jurisdiction for the final actions that were made. I felt very inferior and belittled in the situation.

During the college application process, admission officers have ultimate control over whether you meet the standards to be admitted in to a school that you want to go to. Being rejected from schools made me feel as though all my efforts were not good enough and it was frustrating to feel as though some faceless person was determining my future and held such authority in such a large part of my life.

When applying to the University of Virginia, the Dean of Admissions had the power over whether or not I got into the university.  She was in a position to evaluate my resume and credentials. I felt nervous and anxious until I received my acceptance letter.

It was ski team elections last year.  We were choosing who would be on the executive board for the team this year.  It was crowded, and it was fun to be around everyone, but it wasn't fun choosing.  All of the candidates were very well suited for the positions and I knew them fairly well.  Picking one over the other was not just a difficult decision, but also came with a little guilt feeling like you were betraying one of the candidates who was your friend.

The last time I was in power was when I was completing my chemistry lab report with my group. It was at nighttime (10pm) and the report was due the next morning at 9:30. My lab partners were utterly confused on what happened in the lab at the molecular level, and I had to explain the entire procedure and results to them. Of course, they listened to me completely when I told each person what they had to write. It felt good to be looked up to and respected, however it was a bit annoying that people couldn't pick up their own weight.

The power of someone being in a position to evaluate me was present in my upbringing, as well as in school. I personally think that evaluation in the school system is not necessary, because school systems such as in Norway don't assign grades, yet are rated #1 in the world. Regardless, I feel like the presence of evaluation helped me do better in school. It only affected how I thought consciously when I felt that the evaluation was unfair.

teaching children English as part of a community service project. Despite the fact that as a teacher i was in the  position of power, due to the different levels of engagement by the children some listen to my command more ofter/better than others. Though i would have expected to feel respected or admired, I felt quite the opposite:being in a position of power meant i had a responsibility. Though i was evaluating them, i felt like they were instead evaluating me as a teacher.
Admissions Committee to UVA. They were able to decide if I was going to be accepted here or not and it made me feel very helpless because there wasn't much I could do.

One night me and my friends were in D.C. and it was late at night, I could have told them that we had to go home because we were all spending the night at my house but I instead decided that staying and visiting friends that were in town was more important.

When I worked at my job over the summer, my boss had power over me. Since my boss had control over whether or not I could keep the job and how much I got paid, I was very careful to please her and do a good job. I felt like I had to work extra hard.

I was the chairperson of an event's registration committee. From my position, I was supposed to have a say in the committee's matters, but it turned out that others above me had more power and told me what can and cannot be done. For example, I was not allowed to process and record the checks, grouping people in rooms, and set deadlines. I was only there for the purpose of being a mediator between the people above and the people registering for the event. I felt undermined and unjust because I was capable of doing all of those things.

My senior year of high school, I served as the president of the Key Club. At the end of the year I was given the job of selecting students for the four officer positions for the following school year. I didn't like this part of the job because I knew most of the applicants and thought that all of them were equally good candidates for the positions but I could only select four people.
In volleyball tryouts, I was being evaluated on my skill level and my coach held power over me in determining what team I would be training with for the season. I felt pressure to perform.

I played tennis at an academy. There were 8 of us. We all wanted to play an event but only 3 of us could play. the coaches decided who was going to play. The feeling was hostile between the kids. I felt like I was always watching my back. Never can relax.

I feel like this when I turn in tests, I want to get good grades on all my assignments but I feel like professors and TAs truly have the final say in my grades. Sometimes it makes me feel helpless, even when I have studied very hard for and exam.

I was working at the restaurant as a server for 4 years. After several months, I started training them to get familiarized to the work environment. I explained them to what to do properly, especially how to serve food, customers, and other things that were required to work at the restaurant. It was such a good experience to teach them since that makes me to care about my job and teach myself to inform them in a better way.
i was president of the environmental club and had to pick applicants from a pool to join the committee

Over the summer, I spent some time with my younger cousins who are 9 and 12 years old. Because I am much older than them, I was in a position of power, meaning I could get them to do pretty much whatever I wanted them to do. If I told them to clean something up, they would do it. If I wanted them to go deal with a problem, they would do it without complaining very much. it felt good to see that they respected me, but I also felt somewhat guilty for having them do certain tasks either because I was too lazy to do them myself or because I knew they would not say no.

I was individually evaluated for a clarinet ensemble by complete strangers. The grade they gave me on the performance affected how far I would advance in my school's band. The situation made me feel very nervous, but I got top scores on my performance.

I feel like I'm in a position of power when people come to me for advice, because they then value my opinion. I feel important and like I could make a difference. It is also a responsibility, which can be stressful, but mostly it just makes me happy and empowered.

This past summer I worked as a summer camp counselor. I was put in charge, along with a co-counselor, of ten 12-year-old boys which meant I bore a lot of power and responsibility. One aspect which gave me power was regarding discipline. Some kids were poorly behaved and I would need to determine how to deal with it. Sometimes I would be lenient, but others I would take action and remove them form activities. It made me feel bad to be harsh, but I felt I deserved respect.
in fantasy football i had a player someone else wanted. i had the ability to give them what thjey wanted but i witheld it because i knew i could use it to get myself something good. i liked it,.

There was a time when I was extremely sick. I was not able to get out of bed so my younger siblings were led to do everything I wanted them to. If I wanted a cold glass of water, I would simply have one of my siblings fetch it for me. Although I was feeling miserable because of my illness, I felt incredibly pleased to have my siblings listen to my every request. There was a sense of superiority but also I felt loved. My siblings loved me so much, they wanted to do what I could not do, for me.
Parental discretion regarding whether or not I'd be allowed to travel over spring break; my mother and father were in positions of authority and had the final say.
I felt weak and I kept getting angry as I though it was not fair. I cried because of how angry I was

A position in which I did not have power was my junior year on the baseball team. I had been a starter for two and a half years but was going through a slump. The coach benched me for a game because I was not playing well at second base. He did not put me in the outfield when I was clearly better than the current starter because the other kid's dad was a big donor to the program. I felt extremely angry and cheated at the time. I wanted to quit but my parents didn't let me. Once I realized I couldn't quit the situation motivated me to prove the coach wrong. Eventually everything worked out as I got my spot back and ended up winning MVP.

I was the captain of my most recent soccer. I used my captains authority to control some of the actions of my teammates to better our playing style. i used my captains authority to increase our chances of winning. Also, I used the captain title to be a figure head for our team as someone that my teammates could count on, trust, and come to with anything that might be bothering them.

One incident in which I did not have power or control over a situation was during the summer. This involved my cousin. I spent at a night over her house. However, I ended up spending up to 3 days over. She would not let me leave. I had other tasks to do. Procrastinating on these task stressed me out. I told her of my situation, but she blew it off as insignificant as well as poked fun of me. I felt annoyed and angry at her.  It also wasn't easy to leave because I needed a car to drive home, which she had. As a result of this situation, I ended up disliking her for a period of time. However, I did eventually got over my feelings.
When I was rushing. All I could do was try to impress people. But they had the power to decide the result

When I was in the semifinals of a singing competition and we,all of the seminalists, had finished singing and were just waiting to see who got to the finale. I felt very much out of control at this point and completely anxious of hearing the jury's decision. Time passed by much more slowly and I had all of my attention and focus on what and when will the jury say who got to the next round.

A situation where I found myself powerless was when I turned in my college applications to the universities I wanted to attend. I had no power over their choice of admission, therefore I felt extremely anxious. To add to the anxiousness, the reveal of admission was months after I actually turned in my application so the suspense was at an all time high. Luckily, I got into every university I applied to.

My professors have power over me in class and when I hand in assignments all the time. At times this can be very frustrating because the assignments and tests can conflict with other things in my life and I have no power to change them. It can also be frustrating that they have control over my grades.

A situation in which someone had power over me was my parents not letting me hang out with my friends when I was very young. I felt very annoyed that they had power over me but at the same time respected my parents and knew that I had to listen to them.

My family and I were going to a festival and I had something else planned in mind to do that day. I was highly upset, more than I really should have. Looking back at what happened, I acted childish for my age. After leaving the festival in 20 minutes, I got in trouble for acting the way I did.

One situation in which someone had the power over me was when I went to a job interview in July. They asked me a series of questions to figure out if I would be the right fit with the company or not. I remember becoming very nervous because the interviewers had the power to either give me the job or go with someone else. Having said that, I got a call back and was informed that I received the position and I have been working with the company ever since.

I was the President of my high school's National Honor Society. This club was seen as intense, strict, and rigid to the members, and I was in the position to enforce the strictness and make decisions. I had the power to grant or deny my peers "hours" for doing various tutoring and activities, and it had to be approved by me. It was stressful because I was held accountable for any mistakes that occurred but it also made me feel empowered and at a higher status among my peers

Once, a friend of mine never went to a class that we both were taking. He had none of the notes and had no idea what was going on when it was time for the exam. He came to me begging for help. I had the power to tell him what I wanted and when I wanted. He had to accommodate my schedule. I felt good. He needed me much more than I needed him.

In order to graduate from high school, all seniors must have a sheet of paper signed by all of their teachers, department heads, and finally the principal. The principal has the final say in whether someone graduates or not. I was waiting in line to get my final signature and I felt powerless because my ability to graduate, which was something that I wanted, rested in the hand of one person. There was nothing I could do to change the outcome. The principal looked over my grades, my community service requirements, and my college acceptance letter before he finally signed my sheet. I felt nervous because I did not know what would happen. I ended up graduating, but the thought that I might not be able to just because one person had the power to say no made me feel very inferior.
I was in a situation of power as the captain of my lacrosse team. I felt good about being in a position of power because I knew that I could push my team towards accomplishing our goals.

I was teacher's assistant when I was in middle school. Many of the math exam papers were graded by me, and I was by then quite excited when grading those papers, especially when I could pick out small errors in the procedures written by those really intelligent students. It gave me a sense of superiority as if I was better than my peers.

I was a dance teacher in charge of groups of young children. I was in the position to teach them, guide them, or punish them if they were misbehaving. I liked being in control, but the pressure to do the right thing while being a teacher is somewhat stressful. In a normal class, I would begin by standing in front of the children and discussing what we were going to do during that day's lesson. Then I would lead them to stretch or begin a game. The louder and more restless the children became, the less sure I felt about controlling them. However, if they were acting very quiet and calm, it was easier to teach them.

I was freshman class president at my high school. It was a little intimidating having authority in a class of kids I didn't know at first. It ended up being a really good experience though because I really got to make a difference for our class. I felt proud of what we got accomplished that year and I was excited that I was able to work with other members of my class to plan things for the year.

During Club Soccer Tryouts I was being evaluated by the members of the current team in terms of my skill level. I tried very hard to impress them - harder perhaps than if I was not being evaluated. I felt like I had minimal power in their perception of my skill level considering there were around 200 other guys trying out for the team.

I am an RA. When people were being loud in the common area, I told them to turn the TV volume down. They said they would do it later, but I made them do it immediately. I felt very empowered and a little vindictive toward them. Afterward, I worried if they would not like me anymore.

My dance team captain refused to let me skip night practice to study for my tests. I felt trapped and worried that I wouldn't have time to study, because I had other classes to go to and I had to sleep. I wanted to do well on my exams, but that was being controlled by the captain.

My senior year of high school I was president of the state student council association. As President, I opened up my sessions with icebreakers to make everyone in the meeting more at ease. I had control of everyone's actions as they participated in the icebreakers. It was a pleasant feeling to be in control because I knew by doing so I was bringing everyone together and creating a better environment of ideas and exchange of knowledge.

I work as a nanny in the summer, and I take care of two girls. I am in a position of power when I'm taking care of them because I have the power to make them clean their rooms, go play outside, etc. For example, one day this past summer they wanted to have a friend over but I told them they couldn't because they hadn't cleaned their rooms yet like they were supposed to. They were sad at first, which made me feel a little guilty, but I also felt responsible because I was making sure they got done what they needed to do.

Last year I was in Photojournalism at my high school. It was my first year in the class and one of my best friends was an editor of they yearbook and she convinced me to take the class. Around December I was taken off my original team and placed in charge of a different team who was having trouble. I had to approve the designs of spreads, the placement of picture, edit copy and text, manage the creation of graphics, decide who would cover events, what pictures where good pictures, who to get quotes from, what questions to ask people, the list goes on and on. I was in charge of 8 practically incompetent people, and when they did not do their job right it was my responsibility to fix it. I would stay after school until 9pm, skip my lunch breaks, etc just to get it done right. They would listen to what I told them but I guess it never processed right because, no matter how many times I explained exactly what I wanted, they would never get it right. My team members would listen to me freak out (and I mean yelling and cursing-one time I even cried) and my friends in the class would empathize, but they were going through almost the same thing. The faculty adviser and the editors knew that there was a problem with my team and they tried to help but couldn't. My friends would joke that I had become a dictator and on my paper plate award they used the hash-tag, #ameliaocracy. The final product of the yearbook was not worth the stress that probably took away years of my life. Its so cliche but with great power comes great responsibilities-and unless you have a great team, to get things right, you have to do everything yourself because its your ass on the line not theirs.

I was in a position of power when I was the leader of a student-run literary publication club at my high school.  I had a ton of work to do to make sure that the club went smoothly and the publication at the end of the year was the best that it could be, but it was very rewarding and empowering in the end.  It created a sense of pride, since I put in most of the work and directed other people in ways that they could help me.

I guess an incident would be when I had my interview with a Yale alumni. We were at a coffeeshop downtown and it felt really intimidating because depending on what he wrote about me and my responses to my questions could either hurt or help me get into the university. It made me really nervous. I think it went well but I didn't get accepted.

My senior year of high school I was taking a final for one of my AP classes.  While taking the final I misread the directions and instead of responding to two essay questions I only responded to one.  I did not realize until I had already submitted the exam that I had made this mistake, and I tried to plead with my teacher to let me retake the exam, as I was sure that if I had the opportunity I would have answered the questions correctly.  My teacher however, would not listen to me, in spite of all of my pleas, and refused to let me retake the exam.  I felt helpless, frustrated, and very anxious.  I got a D on the final and was devastated.

My senior year, my tennis coach asked me to help him decide which final girl to cut from tryouts, since I was the captain. I felt very guilty, but obligated to give my opinion because I was the only one in that position.

I was put into this kind of situation when I had my back injury. I could not control my workout schedule, or participate in sports because it was painful. I felt so depressed and helpless because being fit and athletic is important to me. Not being able to participate was heart wrenching. It was difficult to watch my team members succeed while sitting on the sidelines not being able to participate.

I was on an club's executive board in high school and thus controlled, at least in part, the activities of the club and the members of the club.  I enjoyed having this position of authority because I was very invested in the club and I did not want anyone else to mess anything up for anyone else.  The position also helped to boost my confidence level.

When you work as the leader of a club, you have the ability to control who gets in the club, who will be rejected from the club, as well as the actions of the club as a whole. Bringing in new members requires reviewing applications and sometimes conducting interviews. Even if you know a person that is applying, you have to put aside any feelings you have for them as to make an objective decision.

When playing field hockey, my coach consistently held power over my position and whether or not I would start in the next game. This made me feel uneasy and as though I always had to prove myself worthy.

After the last chem lab project each person anomalously evaluated the other  members of their group. Here I had the power to affect their grade by what how I responded. The main conflicts I had were between being nice and being accurate. I wondered how they had scored me or how they would have had I showed up late. Would my groups members have been lenient? Should I? I erred toward nice in my evaluations.

A particular incident in which someone else has had power over me would be in a scholarship interview. In this instance they asked me several questions about a variety of topics such as extracurricular activities, honors, awards, etc. I was nervous because the situation was important to me and I wanted to do well.
I was in a position of power when I was babysitting a little girl. I felt good because I was able to control the situation.

My professor had power over me at one point. I had done well in the class and received an A as my final grade for both semesters for the class, but I had a poor attendance rate to lecture. One of my main motivations for doing well in the class was to be asked to be a teaching assistant for the next year, but the professor's ultimate decision was to not invite me. I suspect my poor attendance to be the cause of this and I have regretted my absence in the class ever since.

One time in a high school biology class, we had to evaluate each others presentations and our grade depended on how our classmates evaluated us. Sometimes it seemed like people gave out grades based on how they judged a person instead of how they judged a person's project. I didn't like leaving the fate of my grade to a bunch of hormonal teenagers. and it made me feel like they were grading me on my looks and the way I talked instead of the information I was conveying.

When I was auditioning to be in the top band my freshman year in high school (for the following year), I thought I had a fantastic audition. Unfortunately, I was only placed in the second highest band; thus, having no control over which band I truly wanted to be in.

I cannot remember a specific experience of power, but sometimes my boyfriend will want me something from me and I am in a position of power.  It feels good to have control over something.  Also it feels very comforting because you can be certain of an outcome.

When I'm in a wrestling match against someone I'm beating I feel in control. I know what they are going to do before they do it. I feel superior and also relaxed because I know how the situation is going to play out.

i was a coach for a soccer team. I was able to control or influence how each player played and how they were able to learn based off of what i thought them.  It felt good because I was able to pass down what i knew.  The feeling to impart knowledge onto another being is a good one. Furthermore, being the coach I was able to make decisions that affected the happiness of the players by deciding who would get to play and not play based off of their performance. It was difficult at times, but overall it was a rewarding experience for myself and the players

A situation in which I did not have power was in my math class junior and senior year of high school. I studied like crazy and yet still could not obtain the grade I desired. I felt completely helpless, frustrated, and panicked. I studied for increasingly greater quantities of time and still my grade would not go up. In the end, I had to pretty much just accept that I would not be able to control my grade and that I had to just pretty much deal with it.

My roommate is really witty and is good at jokes. I do stupid stuff. One day I did something really stupid (it was fun though) and he kept making fun of me to everyone in my hall. I really wanted to get him back and kept thinking of jokes but he kept coming back with better ones. :(

When I was the captain of my high school dance team, our sponsor was beyond over-controlling when it came to decisions for the team. As captain, I felt like she didn't believe I had the intellectual ability to lead the team on my own or make executive decisions for the good of the squad. Basically she controlled every single decision in the group, and when I tried to assert my own leadership, she shot me down every time and chastised me. I felt powerless and so angry. It was frustrating having the title of captain and not being able to even use it. So when she finally asked me to step down as captain, I just was hurt and insulted.

I was in a position of power through SCA in high school. There was a particular project we did were we had to paint a wall with a design that would be up for the whole school year. I was always in charge of this, created the design, and instructed people on what jobs to perform while painting. I didn't necessarily like having to tell other people what to do or dealing with conflict that occurred during the painting. I wanted everyone to be happy with the design, but of course it was impossible to make this happen.

Often times I experience a loss of power with my parents. Growing up, I learned that elders demand respect, however, it often conflicted with my wants and passion. One particular incident I recalled occurred roughly four years ago. I was embarking on my sixth year of dance and my mom confronted me, stating that I should spend more time on my studies. Even though I wished to continue dancing, my parents exerted power over me by discontinuing my dance classes. I felt disheartened, and to this day, I wish I had continued dancing.

My senior year of high school, I was president of the Student Council. I felt very honored to be given this position. My peers and I were able to make positive changes in my school while working with the faculty and staff. Knowing that I was a big part of this made me feel very good inside and proud.

Someone on my hall was locked out of the dorm so she called me to let her in and told me no one else was picking up their phone so I went downstairs and stood inside the door and I could've just gone back upstairs and not let her in. Obviously I let her in but it was nice to be needed for something, to control something.

When applying to college, many individuals evaluated my performance in High School as well as how active I was in the community.  It was stressful because looking back, I realized what I could have done to make my application look stronger.  If only I had studied a little harder for that test, spent a little more time on that paper, got a little more involved in a certain club...etc.  It was probably the first time a large part of my future was out of my hands and placed into the hands of someone else.

Not being in power is scary at times, but it's a part of life. There are always going to be people in charge of you and telling you what to do. Although when they abuse this power or they are rude it can be demeaning and uncomfortable. I have a boss right now that can be very rude to me at times and it generally makes me upset when he does it. It's not just being a bad boss, it's being a bad person.
I was the shotcaller of a league of legends team. i felt as if i had much more responsibility. it was harder to manage my own self because i was focused on everyone else too, and the bigger picture.

This past summer I was traveling and did not have my own car so I had to rely on my boss for a ride. This was fine in terms of going to and from work but at night if I wanted to go get food and needed to run any errands I did not have the ability to do it without her either dropping me off or letting me use her car. It was incredibly frustrating because she would ask me to do favors for her which required that I have access to a car but would not give me the car so I had to find other people to give me rides.

While lifeguarding this summer, I was constantly in a position of power over everyone in and around the pool since I controlled who was allowed in and out of the pool as well as what people were allowed to do while in the pool. It was incredibly boring, the only power I ever actually exercised was telling kids not to run, and I grew annoyed with the kids by the end of the summer.

I remember when I had extra tickets for my graduation ceremony and my friends needed some for their family. I immediately noticed the power I had over them I decided to enjoy this situation for as long as I could. I made them get me food and fight with other over these tickets. Eventually it came down to a bid of how much I would sell the tickets for and I made quite a profit at the end of the day. I was just having a blast being place in that position and didn't feel any type of guilt.
Maybe giving other people interviews is that of a particular incident. I was also really nervous to think that what questions should I ask and I was the representative for us.

I was planning my birthday party at my apartment and I was able to dictate things to my roommates. It was somewhat stressful trying to convince them to do things that I wanted as opposed to what they preferred.

When I was preparing for the SATs in high school my parents made me go to many different prep academies every week. I had no say in whether I should go or not, and at the time I felt very forced and suppressed
I won a bet the other day on the golf course. As payment for losing, my friend had to buy my dinner. I felt like I was in power when he paid for my meal.

when I was little I really wanted a horse, but my mom is scared of horses and wouldn't let us get a horse. She had power over us to say no. In the end she let me do horse-back riding (which was exciting) but still no owning of a horse.

I have been in a position of power regarding housing for next year. I am currently debating two different housing situations where both parties would be benefit with one more person in the house. As both parties' housing situations depend on my decision, I feel the need to evaluate both situations in a fair manner that benefits all parties involved, including myself. As an incentive to pay attention to the lessons and participate in answering questions, I would reward correct answers to the Trivia questions with a single piece of candy the children could select from a variety in a box. My thoughts at each session were "I really hope the kids were paying attention last week, so we don't take more than 10-15 minutes to answer seven questions...". I was hopeful in wishing the kids to actually learn useful, important life lessons as well as enjoying the reward of candy and having fun, but at the same time, I was also used to them having no idea and simply guessing, giving general answers like, "Jesus!" or "God". I felt horrible when they gave the wrong answers, because I would have to reply, "Nope, sorry, that's not quite it", "Want to try again?" with no results. Despite feeling a little guilty when the kids were disappointed in getting the answer wrong (potential for embarrassment there, I suppose) and especially for not receiving candy, I understood that I was the teen leader and was a role model, and couldn't act "flaky" or "wishy-washy" with the kids and just give them the candy whenever they gave a off-the-mark answer. If they were rewarded every time they knowingly gave incorrect or incredibly vague answers, they would not benefit at all from the activity, and wouldn't come away from church having learned important lessons. I felt the position of power to be a slightly undesirable yet necessary role.
